statement: In Oklahoma you petition the district court in the county where you live for a change of name, as long as you have lived in that county for more than 30 days.
detail: Oklahoma law bars anyone required to register under the Oklahoma Sex Offenders Registration Act from petitioning for a name change. If the person is a minor, the petition is brought by a guardian or next friend instead.

cost.note: The statute doesn't set a specific filing fee; contact the district court clerk in your county for the current amount.

source.title: Oklahoma Statutes Citationized — 12 O.S. § 1631, Right to Petition for Change of Name

topic: Oklahoma driver's license and ID name change
statement: You cannot change the name on your Oklahoma driver's license or ID card online. For a name change, you visit a licensed operator or Service Oklahoma (SOK) location in person to request a duplicate, and a new credential is mailed to you for $25.
detail: This help-center article doesn't list which documents to bring for a name change specifically; contact Service Oklahoma or a licensed operator for current requirements.

cost.note: The $25 is Service Oklahoma's standard duplicate-credential fee — the same one charged for other changes, not a fee specific to name changes.

source.title: Service Oklahoma Help Center — How can I make changes to the information on my Driver's License card?

topic: Oklahoma driver's license and ID sex/gender designation
statement: Service Oklahoma's own list of driver's license and ID services does not include a way to change the sex or gender marker on a license or ID card.
detail: This page lists every standard driver's-license and ID service Service Oklahoma offers — a new license, renewals, REAL ID, address updates, and more — and none of them is described as a sex or gender-designation change. Read the current official page yourself, and don't assume a route exists that isn't listed there. A companion record covers Executive Order 2023-20, the governor's 2023 order on how state agencies must define sex.

topic: Oklahoma Executive Order 2023-20 on the definition of sex
statement: Executive Order 2023-20 is an order from Oklahoma's governor, J. Kevin Stitt. It was filed with the Secretary of State on August 1, 2023. It tells every state agency, board, and commission how to define "sex" when they write rules, enforce decisions, or decide disputes: a natural person's "biological sex, either male or female at birth." It also defines "female," "male," "woman," "girl," "man," "boy," "mother," and "father" by the body's reproductive system.
detail: The order also says that any state agency that collects vital statistics — for anti-discrimination laws, or for health, crime, economic, or other data — must record each person as male or female as the order defines them. It lets agencies offer services in single-sex settings where the law allows. The order does not mention driver's licenses, ID cards, or Service Oklahoma by name. A companion record covers what Service Oklahoma's own list of services says. Confirm the current position with Service Oklahoma before relying on either.

source.title: Oklahoma Secretary of State — Executive Order 2023-20 (filed August 1, 2023)

statement: A legal name change on an Oklahoma birth record is not treated as a minor correction — the Oklahoma State Department of Health says a District Court order is required, and you should contact your local court clerk or an attorney for help.
detail: Small mistakes, like a misspelled name, go through the page's own amendment process instead: you send the amendment application (the page's 'Order by Mail' link is OSDH's Birth Certificate Request Form), a $15 fee, a copy of a valid ID, and a short statement explaining the mistake; then you get either an administrative order from OSDH's Administrative Law Court or a district court order; then, once Vital Records has the order, you pay a $25 amendment fee and the amended certificate is issued. An actual legal name change, an adoption, or a paternity update are not minor corrections — they require a District Court order first — and the page says all legal changes to a record can take up to 4 months.

cost.note: The page doesn't state a separate fee for the District Court order path; the $15 application fee and $25 amendment fee it lists are the two payments in its own amendment process. OSDH's request form itself prints a single combined amendment fee — see the companion record.

timeline.note: This is the department's stated ceiling for legal changes generally (adoptions, paternity, and delayed registrations included), not a name-change-specific estimate.

source.title: Oklahoma State Department of Health — Amending an Oklahoma Birth or Death Record

topic: Oklahoma birth certificate amendment fee on OSDH's request form
statement: The Oklahoma State Department of Health's Birth Certificate Request Form lists a single $40.00 one-time initial fee for "delayed registration, amendment, paternity, adoption, or legitimation requests," which includes one certified copy of the record.
detail: The same form lists a standard certified copy at $15 each (a non-refundable, non-transferable record search fee that includes one certified copy if the record is found; additional copies are $15 each), says processing time may be 7-10 business days, that all fees expire one year after the date paid, and that you may send a maximum of five applications per order or envelope. The form must be fully completed and signed, with a photocopy of a current, valid photo ID, full payment, and proof of eligibility, or it will not be processed. OSDH's amendments web page describes the same amendment cost as two payments — see the companion record.

cost.note: One-time initial fee for an amendment request, including one certified copy; additional certified copies are $15 each.

timeline.typical: processing time may be 7-10 business days

source.title: Oklahoma State Department of Health, Vital Records — Birth Certificate Request Form

statement: Oklahoma law says every birth certificate amended under this statute must show the sex identified at the time of birth, and it cannot be amended to display gender identity, a nonbinary designation, or the letter "X".
detail: This rule applies to any amendment made under 63 O.S. § 1-321, not only ones related to gender. Oklahoma law describes no court-order or administrative process for changing the sex designation on a birth certificate to match your gender identity. If you were told a route exists, verify it directly with the Oklahoma State Department of Health before relying on it.

source.title: Oklahoma Statutes Citationized — 63 O.S. § 1-321, Amendment of Certificate or Record
